Chapter 2Delayed Public Signals and Asynchronous Learning

Public information often arrives after private learning has already occurred. Earnings releases, official statistics, and market-wide disclosures are public signals, but different agents may receive them with different delays after acting on partial private information. Delay creates a disclosure window during which a private action can move what others infer; at its known end the manipulation loses its effect.

Extending the noise-state filtering and adjoint system to this timing requires centering the arriving delayed signal: at time t, player i observes dZt−Δi​​ with the part it could already predict subtracted, so the delayed signal arrives as an innovation. The resulting filter kernel has two births, the private-signal birth at u=t and the public-signal birth at u=t−Δi​.

Linear-quadratic stochastic differential games with delay have been studied with the delay in the controls [28]; delayed observation of shared information is the delayed-sharing pattern of decentralized control [88, 111, 117]. Here the delay is in the observation of a public signal, so it enters the filtering and adjoint kernels rather than the state dynamics. The same equations cover the opposite timing, an action that is seen at once but takes effect after a lag τi​, as with time to build [70] or a purchase that is resold later. A delayed action changes the state dynamics and the first-order condition; the filter is untouched.

Section 2.1 sets up the delayed observation, Sections 2.2 and 2.3 derive the filter and verify it, and Section 2.4 prices the arrival in the adjoints and the first-order condition.

2.1Delayed observation structure

Fix a finite player set I={1,…,n} and choose an arbitrary player i. Throughout this chapter, i denotes the player whose filter or control is described, while k∈I∖{i} denotes an opponent or another observer.

Player i observes a private signal dYti​=(Cˉi,Y(t)+∫0t​Ci,Y(t,s)dWs​)dt+EidWt​.(2.1.1) There is also a public signal dZt​=(CˉZ(t)+∫0t​CZ(t,s)dWs​)dt+EZdWt​.(2.1.2) Each player may observe the public signal with a different delay. Player i’s delay is Δi​≥0, and Fti​=σ(Yri​:r≤t)∨σ(Zr​:r≤t−Δi​). The common-delay case is Δ1​=⋯=Δn​=Δ. In applications the public drift kernel CZ may contain state, predictable-control, and uncontrolled components, CZ(t,s)=BXZ​(t)Xt​(s)+m∑​BmZ​(t)DW,tm​(s)+UtZ​(s),(2.1.4) where control-dependent drifts use predictable controls Dt−m​.

The state may also carry delayed control rows,

dXt​=(BXX​(t)Xt​+m∑​BmX​(t)Dtm​+m∑​B~mX​(t)Dt−τm​m​)dt+σ(t)dWt​,Dsm​:=0 (s<0),τm​≥0,(2.1.5)

with B~mX​(s):=0 for s>T. A control chosen at t−τm​ depends only on noise born by then, so in the kernel state equation the delayed row is B~mX​(t)1{s≤t−τm​}​DW,t−τm​m​(s), and the mean equation gains B~mX​(t)Dˉt−τm​m​. The filtering results below do not change. Dt−τm​m​ adds no martingale term to dX; the delayed rows therefore enter the drift kernels Ci,Y and CZ only through Xt​(s). With B~mX​≡0 everything reduces to Chapter 1.

Assumption 2.1 (orthogonal delayed public news). The private and public martingale rows are normalized and orthogonal: EiEi,⊤=I,EZEZ,⊤=I,EiEZ,⊤=0.(2.1.6) Private rows do not directly measure EZdW. Players may infer part of EZdWt−Δi​​ indirectly through earlier drift effects, but this inference is predictable at t−, so it changes only the drift of the arriving Z-innovation, not its instantaneous covariance.

Let sti​:=t−Δi​. At time t, the arriving public increment for player i is dZsti​​ when t≥Δi​. Define the pre-arrival projection of a primitive kernel K by (Pt−i​K)(u):=K(u)Πi+1{u<sti​}​K(u)ΠZ+∫0t​K(r)Ft−i​(r,u)dr,(2.1.7) where Πi=Ei,⊤Ei and ΠZ=EZ,⊤EZ. The strict inequality excludes the just-arriving coordinate u=sti​. The complement (I−Pt−i​)K is the part of K that player i has not resolved before the arrival.

The private unresolved row is Cti,Y​(u):=(I−Pt−i​)[Ci,Y(t,⋅)](u).(2.1.8) Define the centered delayed-public innovation row Cti,Z​(u):=1{t≥Δi​}​((I−Pt−i​)[CZ(sti​,⋅)](u)−EZFt−i​(sti​,u)).​(2.1.9) Since EZFt−i​(t−Δi​,⋅) need not vanish, player i also subtracts its predictable estimate of the arriving Z-noise increment. The delayed-public innovation is dIti,Z​​:=1{t≥Δi​}​(dZsti​​−E[dZsti​​∣Ft−i​])=1{t≥Δi​}​EZdWsti​​+∫0t​Cti,Z​(u)dWu​dt.​(2.1.10)​ Similarly, dIti,Y​:=dYti​−E[dYti​∣Ft−i​]=EidWt​+∫0t​Cti,Y​(u)dWu​dt.(2.1.11) By (2.1.6), dIti,Y​ and dIti,Z​ have block-identity instantaneous covariance and no mixed quadratic variation. Figure 2.1 shows the geometry.

2.2Filtering with delayed public signals

The theorem verifies a candidate kernel, taking the representation as given and deriving the equations it must satisfy. Existence of a kernel with the representation is part of the equilibrium fixed point and is not claimed here.

Theorem 2.2 (Filtering with a delayed public innovation row). For each i∈I, let Δi​ be a known constant delay, maintain Assumption 2.1, and suppose a deterministic kernel Fi is such that the candidate noise-state has the representation du​Wti​(u)=ΠidWu​+1{u<t−Δi​}​ΠZdWu​+(∫0t​Fti​(u,s)dWs​)du.(2.2.1) Define Ci,Y and Ci,Z by (2.1.8) and (2.1.9). Away from the two birth lines u=t and u=t−Δi​, Fi satisfies ∂t​Fti​(u,s)=Cti,Y​(u)⊤Cti,Y​(s)+Cti,Z​(u)⊤Cti,Z​(s).(2.2.2) The private signal creates the usual birth at u=t, Fti​(u,t)=Cti,Y​(u)⊤Ei,Fti​(t,u)=Ei,⊤Cti,Y​(u),(2.2.3) and the delayed public signal creates a second birth at sti​=t−Δi​, the coordinate whose public news arrives at t, Fti​(u,sti​)​Z​=Cti,Z​(u)⊤EZ,Fti​(sti​,u)​Z​=EZ,⊤Cti,Z​(u).(2.2.4) Equivalently, with noncausal rows and empty integrals equal to zero, Fti​(u,s)=​Csi,Y​(u)⊤Ei+Ei,⊤Cui,Y​(s)+1{s+Δi​≤t}​Cs+Δi​i,Z​(u)⊤EZ+1{u+Δi​≤t}​EZ,⊤Cu+Δi​i,Z​(s)+∫max{u,s}t​Cri,Y​(u)⊤Cri,Y​(s)dr+∫max{u,s}t​Cri,Z​(u)⊤Cri,Z​(s)dr.​(2.2.5)​ With Fi given by (2.2.5), (2.2.1) is the conditional expectation E[Wu​∣Fti​].

2.3Filtering derivation

The argument follows the proof of the baseline filtering theorem, Theorem 1.5. The only new ingredient is that the test martingale has two orthogonal measurement rows and the delayed public news is the centered innovation (2.1.10).

Exponential tests

Fix deterministic test functions rY​,rZ​ and define dϕt​=iϕt​[(dIti,Y​)⊤rY​(t)+(dIti,Z​)⊤rZ​(t)],ϕ0​=1.(2.3.1) The candidate Wti​(u) is the conditional expectation of Wu​ if and only if E[Wti​(u)ϕt​]=E[Wu​ϕt​]for all rY​,rZ​.(2.3.2)

Left-hand side

Write the candidate innovation-form dynamics for a fixed coordinate u as dt​Wti​(u)=BYW,i​(u,t)dIti,Y​+BZW,i​(u,t)dIti,Z​.(2.3.3) Since the two innovation rows have no mixed quadratic variation, Itô’s product rule gives d(Wti​(u)ϕt​)=​iWti​(u)ϕt​(dIti,Y​)⊤rY​(t)+iWti​(u)ϕt​(dIti,Z​)⊤rZ​(t)+ϕt​BYW,i​(u,t)dIti,Y​+ϕt​BZW,i​(u,t)dIti,Z​+iϕt​BYW,i​(u,t)rY​(t)dt+iϕt​BZW,i​(u,t)rZ​(t)dt.​ Using (2.1.11)–(2.1.10) to collect the dt terms, dtd​E[Wti​(u)ϕt​]=​iE[ϕt​(Wti​(u)∫0t​Cti,Y​(r)dWr⊤​+BYW,i​(u,t))]rY​(t)+iE[ϕt​(Wti​(u)∫0t​Cti,Z​(r)dWr⊤​+BZW,i​(u,t))]rZ​(t).​(2.3.5)​ No additional predictable residual appears because Ii,Y and Ii,Z are already centered relative to Ft−i​.

Right-hand side

For the private row, dt1​E[Wu​(dIti,Y​)⊤∣Ft−i​]==​E[Wu​∫0t​Cti,Y​(r)dWr⊤​∣Ft−i​]+Ei,⊤1{u≥t}​Wt−i​(u)∫0t​Cti,Y​(r)dWt−i​(r)⊤+∫0t​∂r​Ct−i​(u,r)Cti,Y​(r)⊤dr+Ei,⊤1{u≥t}​,​(2.3.6)​ where Cti​(u,r)=Cov(Wu​,Wr​∣Fti​). For the delayed public signal, the same calculation applies to the centered innovation (2.1.10). The martingale part arrives at sti​ and the drift row is Ci,Z, so dt1​E[Wu​(dIti,Z​)⊤∣Ft−i​]=​Wt−i​(u)∫0t​Cti,Z​(r)dWt−i​(r)⊤+∫0t​∂r​Ct−i​(u,r)Cti,Z​(r)⊤dr+EZ,⊤1{t≥Δi​}​1{u≥sti​}​.​(2.3.7)​ Combining,

dtd​E[Wu​ϕt​]=iE[ϕt​(Wti​(u)∫0t​Cti,Y​(r)dWti​(r)⊤+∫0t​∂r​Cti​(u,r)Cti,Y​(r)⊤dr+Ei,⊤1{u≥t}​)]rY​(t)∗+iE[ϕt​(Wti​(u)∫0t​Cti,Z​(r)dWti​(r)⊤+∫0t​∂r​Cti​(u,r)Cti,Z​(r)⊤dr+EZ,⊤1{t≥Δi​}​1{u≥sti​}​)]rZ​(t).​(2.3.8)

Coefficient matching

Matching (2.3.5) and (2.3.8) for arbitrary rY​,rZ​ gives BYW,i​(u,t)BZW,i​(u,t)​=∫0t​∂r​Cti​(u,r)Cti,Y​(r)⊤dr+Ei,⊤1{u≥t}​,=∫0t​∂r​Cti​(u,r)Cti,Z​(r)⊤dr+EZ,⊤1{t≥Δi​}​1{u≥sti​}​.​(2.3.9)(2.3.10)​ Differentiating these expressions in the source time u gives, away from jumps, dt​(du​Wti​(u))=Cti,Y​(u)⊤dIti,Y​du+Cti,Z​(u)⊤dIti,Z​du.(2.3.11) Equation (2.3.9) jumps at u=t, giving the private-signal birth, and (2.3.10) jumps at u=sti​, giving the public-signal birth.

Primitive-shock expansion and the two birth terms

Integrating (2.3.11) over observation times gives du​Wti​(u)=​Ei,⊤dIui,Y​+1{u+Δi​≤t}​EZ,⊤dIu+Δi​i,Z​+(∫ut​Cri,Y​(u)⊤dIri,Y​)du+(∫ut​Cri,Z​(u)⊤dIri,Z​)du.​(2.3.12)​ Substitute (2.1.11) and (2.1.10). The direct private term is Ei,⊤dIui,Y​=ΠidWu​+Ei,⊤∫0u​Cui,Y​(s)dWs​du. The direct delayed public term is 1{u+Δi​≤t}​EZ,⊤dIu+Δi​i,Z​=1{u+Δi​≤t}​ΠZdWu​+1{u+Δi​≤t}​EZ,⊤∫0u+Δi​​Cu+Δi​i,Z​(s)dWs​du. The accumulated martingale updates contribute ∫ut​Cri,Y​(u)⊤EidWr​du,∫max{0,u−Δi​}t−Δi​​Cs+Δi​i,Z​(u)⊤EZdWs​du. The accumulated drift updates contribute, by stochastic Fubini, ∫0t​(∫max{u,s}t​Cri,Y​(u)⊤Cri,Y​(s)dr)dWs​du,∫0t​(∫max{u,s}t​Cri,Z​(u)⊤Cri,Z​(s)dr)dWs​du.​ Collecting the coefficient of dWs​du gives (2.2.5). The singular direct terms give the two direct pieces in (2.2.1). The candidate representation satisfies the test identities (2.3.2); uniqueness follows from Itô isometry as in the proof of Theorem 1.5.

2.4First variations and delayed-public adjoints

A deviation misleads private learners today, but the manipulated component resurfaces when the public news arrives at delay Δk​. Player i pays for moving the drift of the delayed public signal when that signal reaches opponent k, and the belief price Hk,i jumps at that date; together these are the marginal cost of that second effect. Each opponent now carries two observation rows, the private row and the centered delayed-public innovation.

Fix the deviating player i and freeze opponents’ strategy maps and filters. For k=i, write δwsk​(u) for the density variation of opponent k’s noise-state and δXs​ for the physical-state variation. The induced opponent-control variation is δDsk​=∫0s​Dsk​(u)δwsk​(u)du.(2.4.1) Opponent k observes at time s the public signal generated at source time qk​=ssk​=s−Δk​. Write δbqk​Z​ for the variation of the predictable drift of that public signal. In the affine example bqk​Z​=BXZ​(qk​)Xqk​​+∑m​BmZ​(qk​)Dqk​−m​+Uqk​Z​, this means δbqk​Z​=BXZ​(qk​)δXqk​​+m=i∑​BmZ​(qk​)∫0qk​​Dqk​m​(r)δwqk​m​(r)dr,(2.4.2) with the right-hand side zero if qk​ lies before the initial perturbation date. The deviating player’s own instantaneous effect through BiZ​(qk​)Dqk​i​ stays out of the forward variation system and enters the first-order condition below directly.

Forward first-variation system

Opponent k’s private residual is ηsk,Y​:=BXY,k​(s)(δXs​−∫0s​Xs​(r)δwsk​(r)dr).(2.4.3) The subtraction leaves the part of the state variation opponent k has not yet inferred. The centered delayed-public residual is ηsk,Z​:=1{s≥Δk​}​(δbqk​Z​−∫0s​CZ(qk​,r)δws−k​(r)dr−EZδws−k​(qk​)),qk​=s−Δk​.(2.4.4) The last term is the first-variation counterpart of the centering correction −EZFs−k​(qk​,⋅) in the delayed-public innovation.

Existing noise-state coordinates satisfy ∂s​δwsk​(u)=Csk,Y​(u)⊤ηsk,Y​+Csk,Z​(u)⊤ηsk,Z​,u<s,(2.4.5) with two birth conditions, one at the current date and one at the arrival date, δwsk​(s)​Y​=Ek,⊤ηsk,Y​,δwsk​(s−Δk​)​Z​=1{s≥Δk​}​EZ,⊤ηsk,Z​.(2.4.6) The physical variation satisfies

dsd​δXs​=BXX​(s)δXs​+k=i∑​BkX​(s)∫0s​Dsk​(u)δwsk​(u)du+k=i∑​B~kX​(s)∫0s−τk​​Ds−τk​k​(u)δws−τk​k​(u)du,(2.4.7)

where δwrk​≡0 before the perturbation date. The last sum in (2.4.7) is what opponent k decided τk​ ago, on the beliefs it held then. The deviating player’s spike now produces two impulses, δXt​=v:=BiX​(t)z when it acts and a jump v~:=B~iX​(t+τi​)z at the effect date. Equations (2.4.3)–(2.4.7) are the delayed-public analogue of the baseline forward variation system.

Forward transfer functions

For s≥t, define the forward transfer functions by the response to initial data (δXt​,δwtm​(⋅)), m=i: δXs​δwsk​(r)​=ΦXX(s,t)v+m=i∑​∫0t​ΦXm(s,t,u)δwtm​(u)du,=ΦkX(s,t,r)v+m=i∑​∫0t​Φkm(s,t,r,u)δwtm​(u)du.​(2.4.8)(2.4.9)​ The initial conditions are ΦXX(t,t)=I,ΦkX(t,t,r)=0,ΦXm(t,t,u)=0,Φkm(t,t,r,u)=1{k=m}​δ(r−u),(2.4.10) where the last identity holds weakly.

Define the residual transfer coefficients obtained by substituting (2.4.8)–(2.4.9) into (2.4.3)–(2.4.4). For a physical initial perturbation v, set YkX(s,t)​:=BXY,k​(s)(ΦXX(s,t)−∫0s​Xs​(r)ΦkX(s,t,r)dr),​(2.4.11)​ and ZkX(s,t)​:=1{s≥Δk​}​[δbqk​;tZ,X​−∫0s​CZ(qk​,r)ΦkX(s−,t,r)dr−EZΦkX(s−,t,qk​)],qk​=s−Δk​,​(2.4.12) where δbqk​;tZ,X​​:=BXZ​(qk​)ΦXX(qk​,t)+ℓ=i∑​BℓZ​(qk​)∫0qk​​Dqk​ℓ​(r)ΦℓX(qk​,t,r)dr,​(2.4.13) with all transfer functions at qk​<t read as zero in the first two terms. Similarly, for an initial belief perturbation in block m, Ykm(s,t,u)​:=BXY,k​(s)(ΦXm(s,t,u)−∫0s​Xs​(r)Φkm(s,t,r,u)dr),​(2.4.14)​ and Zkm(s,t,u)​:=1{s≥Δk​}​[δbqk​;tZ,km​(u)−∫0s​CZ(qk​,r)Φkm(s−,t,r,u)dr−EZΦkm(s−,t,qk​,u)],​(2.4.15) where δbqk​;tZ,km​(u):=BXZ​(qk​)ΦXm(qk​,t,u)+ℓ=i∑​BℓZ​(qk​)∫0qk​​Dqk​ℓ​(r)Φℓm(qk​,t,r,u)dr.(2.4.16)

The transfer functions solve the forward equations ∂s​ΦXX(s,t)∂s​ΦXm(s,t,u)∂s​ΦkX(s,t,r)∂s​Φkm(s,t,r,u)​=BXX​(s)ΦXX(s,t)+k=i∑​BkX​(s)∫0s​Dsk​(r)ΦkX(s,t,r)dr+k=i∑​B~kX​(s)∫0s−τk​​Ds−τk​k​(r)ΦkX(s−τk​,t,r)dr,=BXX​(s)ΦXm(s,t,u)+k=i∑​BkX​(s)∫0s​Dsk​(r)Φkm(s,t,r,u)dr+k=i∑​B~kX​(s)∫0s−τk​​Ds−τk​k​(r)Φkm(s−τk​,t,r,u)dr,=Csk,Y​(r)⊤YkX(s,t)+Csk,Z​(r)⊤ZkX(s,t),=Csk,Y​(r)⊤Ykm(s,t,u)+Csk,Z​(r)⊤Zkm(s,t,u),​(2.4.17)(2.4.18)(2.4.19)(2.4.20)​ for old-history coordinates, those already born and away from the two birth lines, together with the two boundary updates ΦkX(s,t,s)​Y​Φkm(s,t,s,u)​Y​ΦkX(s,t,s−Δk​)​Z​Φkm(s,t,s−Δk​,u)​Z​​=Ek,⊤YkX(s,t),=Ek,⊤Ykm(s,t,u),=1{s≥Δk​}​EZ,⊤ZkX(s,t),=1{s≥Δk​}​EZ,⊤Zkm(s,t,u).​(2.4.21)(2.4.22)​ Transfer functions with a time argument below t are zero, so the delayed rows are inactive until s=t+τk​. The deviating player’s delayed impulse stays outside the forward variation system; by linearity it contributes ΦXX(s,t+τi​)v~.

2.4.1State price, belief prices, and cost variation

Let Lsi​:=GXX,i(s)Xs​+GsX,i​+GXD,i(s)Dsi​,LTi​:=GXX,i(T)XT​+GTX,i​. Lsi​ and LTi​ are the running and terminal marginal costs of the physical state. Pairing the forward state response with future marginal costs gives the state price and the belief prices: HtX,i​Htk,i​(u)​:=∫tT​ΦXX(s,t)⊤Lsi​ds+ΦXX(T,t)⊤LTi​,:=∫tT​ΦXk(s,t,u)⊤Lsi​ds+ΦXk(T,t,u)⊤LTi​,k=i.​(2.4.24)(2.4.25)​ Here ΦXk is the state response to an initial perturbation of opponent k’s noise-state coordinate.

For a control spike z∈L2(Ω,Fti​;Rd), the normalized first variation of player i’s cost is

δJti​(z)=​E[z⊤(GDD,i(t)Dti​+GDX,i(t)Xt​+BiX​(t)⊤HtX,i​+1{t+τi​≤T}​B~iX​(t+τi​)⊤Ht+τi​X,i​)∣Fti​]+E​z⊤BiZ​(t)⊤k=i∑​1{t+Δk​≤T}​(Bk,ZHk,i)t+Δk​←t​∣Fti​​​(2.4.26)​

when the deviating player’s predictable action enters the public-signal drift through BiZ​(t)Dt−i​. If BiZ​≡0, the second line drops out. The new term in the first line is the state price at the effect date.

Backward equations

The two birth conditions of the forward system, at the current date and at the arrival date, enter the backward system through two forms of the filter contraction B of Chapter 1, equation (1.4.9), which contracts a belief price against the observer’s own filter. The filter contraction of the belief price is BkHtk,i​=EkHtk,i​(t)+∫0t​Ctk,Y​(r)Htk,i​(r)dr.(2.4.27) This is the price, for player i, of moving opponent k’s private signal-source drift at time t. For the public row generated at source time s and observed by opponent k at s+Δk​, the delayed contraction Bk,Z is built from the centered public innovation (EZ,Ck,Z); player i pays it at the arrival date s+Δk​, projected on information at the source time s: (Bk,ZHk,i)s+Δk​←s​:=1{s+Δk​≤T}​(EZHs+Δk​k,i​(s)+∫0s+Δk​​Cs+Δk​k,Z​(r)Hs+Δk​k,i​(r)dr).(2.4.28) This is the price of moving the drift of the delayed public signal row generated at source time s, paid when the row reaches opponent k. The first term in each display is the transpose of the birth condition (2.4.6); the integral term is the transpose of the drift update (2.4.5).

Differentiating the transfer representations (2.4.24)–(2.4.25), using the forward equations (2.4.17)–(2.4.22), and collecting the coefficients of δX and δwk gives the equations below. With delayed rows the forward system is a linear delay system, whose adjoint carries advanced arguments; the coefficient of δwtk​(u) then collects the state price at t and at t+τk​. dtd​HtX,i​=−Lti​−BXX​(t)⊤HtX,i​−k=i∑​Vtk,i​,(2.4.29) where Vtk,i​=BXY,k​(t)⊤BkHtk,i​+1{t+Δk​≤T}​BXZ​(t)⊤(Bk,ZHk,i)t+Δk​←t​.(2.4.30) The belief price satisfies, for old-history coordinates other than the one whose public news arrives at t, dtd​Htk,i​(u)=​−(BkX​(t)Dtk​(u))⊤HtX,i​−1{t+τk​≤T}​(B~kX​(t+τk​)Dtk​(u))⊤Ht+τk​X,i​+Xt​(u)⊤BXY,k​(t)⊤BkHtk,i​+1{t≥Δk​}​CZ(t−Δk​,u)⊤(Bk,ZHk,i)t←t−Δk​​−k′=i∑​1{t+Δk′​≤T}​(BkZ​(t)Dtk​(u))⊤(Bk′,ZHk′,i)t+Δk′​←t​.​(2.4.31) When the news about the coordinate u=t arrives, at time t+Δk​, the centered delayed-public innovation adds a jump, dual to the centering term −EZδws−k​(qk​) in (2.4.4): Ht+Δk​−k,i​(t)=Ht+Δk​+k,i​(t)−EZ,⊤(Bk,ZHk,i)t+Δk​←t​.(2.4.32) Equations (2.4.29)–(2.4.32) reduce to the baseline adjoint system when the delayed public signal is absent and B~X≡0. The second term in (2.4.31) is the delayed-action term, the state price at t+τk​, which a backward sweep has already formed. Equation (2.4.29) is unchanged because a delayed control is noise-state linear, so its variation in (2.4.7) is driven by δws−τm​m​ and not by δXs​.

First-order condition

Since the best-response problem is strictly convex in the deviating player’s L2 control, stationarity of (2.4.26) for every z∈L2(Ω,Fti​;Rd) gives GDD,i(t)Dti​+E[​GDX,i(t)Xt​+BiX​(t)⊤HtX,i​+1{t+τi​≤T}​B~iX​(t+τi​)⊤Ht+τi​X,i​+BiZ​(t)⊤k=i∑​1{t+Δk​≤T}​(Bk,ZHk,i)t+Δk​←t​​Fti​]=0.​​(2.4.33) Write Ht+τi​X,i​=Hˉt+τi​X,i​+∫0T​Ht+τi​X,i​(u)dWu​; then E[Ht+τi​X,i​∣Fti​]=Hˉt+τi​X,i​+∫0t​Ht+τi​X,i​(u)dWti​(u), and apart from the public-drift term the equilibrium kernels are

Dti​(u)=−GDD,i(t)−1[GDX,i(t)Xt​(u)+BiX​(t)⊤HtX,i​(u)+1{t+τi​≤T}​B~iX​(t+τi​)⊤Ht+τi​X,i​(u)],u≤t.

The coordinates u∈(t,t+τi​], noise that arrives between the action and its effect, carry no information at t and drop out.

This is the mirror image of the delayed public signal. A delayed action moves opponents’ beliefs when player i takes it and the state when it lands, so the player pays the wedge at t and the state price at t+τi​. An action that opponents see only through the delayed public signal moves the state at t and their beliefs when the news lands, so the player pays the state price at t and the wedge, through Bk,Z, at t+Δk​. Each effect is priced at the date it arrives and projected on the information of the action date. The finite-deviation identity of Corollary 1.11 carries over with the delayed public row and the delayed control rows appended, since both are deterministic causal functionals of the realized control.

2.5Conclusion

Delayed observations add a second birth line, u=t−Δi​ in (2.2.4), to the filter kernel Fi; the noise-state coordinates Wti​(u) are unchanged. Theorem 2.2, the main filtering result, verifies the delayed noise-state filter representation. The two birth lines reappear in the adjoint as the public birth term EZHs+Δk​k,i​(s) in (2.4.28) and the jump at the arrival date (2.4.32), and in the first-order condition (2.4.33) through Bk,Z.
